titulo: The Victory That Was Good for Nothing
subtitulo: Failed hegemonies, mercenaries, and the exhaustion of the polis as a political form (404 – 338 BCE)

coda.heading: Coda for the journey: what to look for

items.text: In Athens, look in the National Archaeological Museum and in the Kerameikos for the fourth-century-BCE funerary stelae and compare them mentally with those of the fifth century. The change is notable: size grows, expenditure grows, the display of family intimacy and private mourning grows. It is the material signature of a society retreating from the public sphere into the domestic one, expressing its hierarchy in funerary marble. Demetrius of Phalerum had to ban them as sumptuary excess around 317 BCE. The monumentalization of private death tends to accompany the hollowing-out of civic life; notice whether you recognize the phenomenon in Lima's cemeteries.

In Corfu, the question to ask in any conversation is who decides. The island has always existed within a system of external protection — Athenian, Roman, Venetian, French, British, European — and its ruling class has always known how to turn that dependency into a resource. It is not servility: it is a rational strategy of a peripheral elite, the same one we study in Peru under the name of creole intermediation. Listen to how people talk about European funds and foreign investment, and about who administers them.

It is also, not coincidentally, the name under which Greece sustained, between 1991 and 2018, one of the most stubborn diplomatic disputes of contemporary Europe.

sections.heading: Sparta wins the war and loses the argument
paragraphs: The previous installment ended in 404 BCE, with the Athenian fleet destroyed and the walls of Piraeus torn down to the sound of flutes. School historiography usually closes the classical cycle there and jumps straight to Alexander. That leap conceals the most instructive period for a sociological reading: the sixty-six years in which the system of poleis attempts, three consecutive times, to produce a stable hegemonic order, and fails three times. What is exhausted between 404 and 338 BCE is not a city or a dynasty: it is an entire POLITICAL FORM.

Let us begin with the founding discomfort. Sparta defeated Athens because Persia paid for its fleet. The Treaty of Miletus and its successive renegotiations handed Cyrus the Younger and the satraps of Anatolia what Salamis had prevented: tutelage over the Greeks of Asia. That is, the power that presented itself as the liberator of Greece from Athenian tyranny financed its victory by selling the Ionian Greeks to the very empire against which, eighty years earlier, the entire legitimacy of the Hellenic world had been built. Here it is worth resisting the temptation to moralize. What matters is not the hypocrisy — hypocrisy is the normal condition of international politics — but the structural fact: no polis had a fiscal base sufficient to sustain a permanent fleet without an external subsidy. The proclaimed AUTONOMY was financially impossible. The entire period that follows is the administration of that impossibility.

Sparta administered its victory with a brutality that eroded its political capital in less than a decade: garrisons (harmosts) and boards of ten oligarchs imposed on the liberated cities, tribute, and, in Athens, the regime of the Thirty, whose terror of 404–403 BCE cost, according to ancient figures, some fifteen hundred deaths in eight months upon a citizenry already decimated. Athenian democracy was restored in 403 with an explicit amnesty — the legal prohibition on "recalling past wrongs," MĒ MNĒSIKAKEIN — one of the first legal devices of compulsory forgetting on record. Four years later that same restored democracy executed Socrates. That sequence — terror, amnesty, restoration, and a persecutory anxiety that seeks out symbolic culprits — is exactly the one that twentieth-century Latin American transitions would retrace. The pact of forgetting is effective for rebuilding institutions and disastrous for processing accountability; Greece will apply it again in 1974, and Peru attempted it, with less success and more impunity, after the internal conflict of 1980–2000.

sections.heading: The King's Peace: Persia as arbiter of Greece (395–386 BCE)
paragraphs: The reaction against Spartan hegemony produced the Corinthian War (395–387 BCE), in which Athens, Thebes, Corinth, and Argos allied against Sparta with Persian gold, exactly as Sparta had defeated Athens with Persian gold. The outcome has a perfect irony and an enormous analytical usefulness: the King's Peace, or Peace of Antalcidas, of 387/386 BCE, was dictated from Susa. The text stipulated that the cities of Asia belonged to the Great King and that the rest would be autonomous, and that whoever did not accept this would have the king as an enemy. For the first time, a Persian document becomes the constitution of the Greek world, and the principle of AUTONOMY — the keyword of the entire Hellenic political vocabulary — appears as an imperial concession, not as a conquest of one's own.

It is worth pausing over the mechanism, because it recurs. General autonomy functioned, in practice, as an instrument of fragmentation: it prevented leagues and confederations, that is, it prevented any aggregation of power capable of challenging the arbiter. Sparta became the enforcer of that clause and used it to dissolve the Boeotian confederacy and occupy the Cadmea of Thebes in 382 BCE in the midst of peace. International law, when guaranteed by a power with its own interests, tends to produce the order that suits the guarantor. It is the same structure we examined in the previous installment regarding the twelve miles of the Ionian Sea, and the same one running through any contemporary discussion of conditionality, investment arbitration, or supranational fiscal oversight. A country can be formally sovereign and be constituted by rules it did not write.

sections.heading: Thebes: the only social revolution of the period (371–362 BCE)
paragraphs: The Theban hegemony lasted barely nine years and is usually treated as an interlude. It was much more than that. At Leuctra, in 371 BCE, Epaminondas defeated the Spartan army with a tactical innovation — the reinforced left wing, fifty ranks deep, the oblique order — that shattered Sparta's myth of hoplite invincibility. But the truly radical decision came afterward. In 370/369 BCE Epaminondas invaded Laconia, something no enemy had done in centuries, and instead of plundering and withdrawing he did the one irreversible thing: he liberated Messenia and founded the city of Messene.

Understanding the weight of that requires recalling what Sparta was. Its system of full-time citizen-warriors rested on the forced labor of the Messenian HELOTS, a population subjugated for some three hundred and fifty years, against whom the ephors formally declared war every year so that killing them would not constitute ritual homicide. Liberating Messenia was not a humanitarian gesture: it was the surgical destruction of a power's material base. Sparta never recovered. It had already been suffering from OLIGANTHROPIA, the decline in the number of full citizens — from some eight thousand at the start of the fifth century to little more than a thousand in the fourth — through land concentration and inheritance rules that expelled from the citizen body anyone who could not pay their share of the common mess. A regime that presented itself as the most egalitarian in Greece collapsed from internal inequality.

The sociological reading is direct and applies to Peru as much as to Greece: no political order survives the silent erosion of the social base that sustains it, however impeccable its institutional facade or its military prestige may be. Sparta was defeated twice, and the first defeat — demographic, agrarian, invisible — preceded Leuctra by several generations. When Epaminondas died at Mantinea, in 362 BCE, Xenophon closed his history with a sentence that is, in itself, a diagnosis of systemic exhaustion: after the battle there was "even more confusion and disorder in Greece than before."

sections.heading: Mercenaries: the citizen-soldier becomes a hired hand
paragraphs: The least visible and most decisive phenomenon of these decades is the professionalization of violence. In 401 BCE, ten thousand Greeks enlisted as mercenaries in the Persian dynastic war of Cyrus the Younger; after the defeat at Cunaxa, they crossed Mesopotamia and Armenia to the Black Sea, and Xenophon turned that retreat into the ANABASIS. The book is usually read as an epic of resistance; read as a social document it is something else: proof that there already existed, at the start of the fourth century BCE, a pan-Hellenic labor market of armed men willing to serve any paymaster, including the traditional enemy.

The cause is economic. The wars of the fifth century had ruined thousands of small landowners; land became concentrated; the demographic surplus could no longer be drained through colonization because the coastlines were already occupied. The result is a surplus of landless, tradeless young men, and a constant demand for them in Persia, in rebellious Egypt, in Sicily, in Macedonia. Isocrates says it bluntly around 346 BCE, proposing a panhellenic crusade to Philip: these men must be taken abroad before they become an internal problem. External war as an escape valve for an internal social crisis is an argument that recurs with depressing regularity throughout history.

The political effect is deeper than the military one. Athenian democracy, as we have seen, was born of the link between military service and citizenship: the poor rower demanded a voice because his body sustained the city. When war is waged by paid professionals and generals who negotiate their own contracts — Iphicrates, Chares, Timotheus operate almost as military entrepreneurs — that link is severed. Citizenship ceases to carry a bodily price and comes to carry a fiscal one. The citizen becomes a taxpayer and a spectator. Anyone observing the contemporary relationship between professional armies, private contractors, and a demobilized public opinion will recognize the transition. In Peru, the effective suspension of mandatory military service and the growing delegation of security functions to private companies produced its own version of that disconnection: security as a service that is purchased, not an obligation that is shared, with the evident consequences in unequal protection between districts.

sections.heading: Philip: the periphery devours the center (359–338 BCE)
paragraphs: Macedonia was, for fifth-century Athenians, a semi-barbarian territory in the north that exported timber for ships and whose kings spoke a dubious Greek. In 359 BCE Philip II comes to the throne after a catastrophic defeat at the hands of the Illyrians, with the kingdom on the verge of dissolution. In twenty years he builds the most effective state that had ever existed in the Greek world, and he does so by combining precisely what the poleis could not combine: a broad territorial base with a peasant population, a monarchy capable of deciding without an assembly, gold mines — Pangaion, after the capture of Amphipolis in 357 BCE, producing a thousand talents a year — and a permanent army trained year-round with the SARISSA, the five-to-six-meter pike that renders the traditional hoplite formation useless.

The decisive observation is that Philip did not defeat the poleis chiefly through military superiority, but through superiority of time. A standing army can campaign in winter; a citizen militia must return for the harvest. A monarchy can sustain a foreign policy across two decades; an assembly changes course every season according to who speaks best that day. Philip bought, bribed, married off daughters, intervened in the Third Sacred War as the defender of Delphi, and thereby obtained a seat on the Amphictyonic Council: he made himself Greek through institutional means before conquering Greece by military ones.

The Athenian debate of those years is one of the richest political discussions of Antiquity and has no obviously correct side. Demosthenes, in the Philippics, holds that freedom is not negotiable and that yielding to Philip out of comfort is the surest way to lose everything. Isocrates responds that the autonomy of the poleis is already a fiction, that they have spent a century destroying one another, and that the only realistic way out is to accept a hegemon capable of imposing peace and turning the violence outward against Persia. One defends a principle that no longer has a material base; the other offers a solution whose price is VOLUNTARY SERVITUDE. At Chaeronea, in 338 BCE, the Macedonian army destroyed the Athenian and Theban forces — the Sacred Band died to the last man on the field — and the following year the League of Corinth formalized a common peace under Macedonian hegemony. The form of the polis survived intact: assemblies, magistrates, festivals, courts. What disappeared was its capacity to decide on war and peace. It is the exact difference between AUTONOMY and SOVEREIGNTY, and it is the difference that organizes everything we will see in the installments to come, up to the year 2026.

sections.heading: The simultaneous world: Susa, Carthage, Rome, the Andes
paragraphs: While Greece bled itself dry, the Achaemenid empire was going through its own dynastic convulsions and reconquered Egypt in 343 BCE after sixty years of independence: it remained, on the eve of its fall, the richest state on the planet. In the western Mediterranean, Carthage and the Syracuse of Dionysius I waged a century-long war over Sicily, also with mercenary armies. And in Latium, in that same year of Chaeronea, 338 BCE, Rome closed out the Latin War and reorganized the defeated peoples with an instrument Greece never invented: EXTENSIBLE CITIZENSHIP, in degrees, including citizenship without voting rights. That technical difference — a political community that can grow by incorporating rather than excluding — explains a good deal of why Rome built a lasting empire while the Greek poleis could not even federate. Athenian citizenship, closed by Pericles's law of 451 BCE to the children of two Athenian parents, was a hereditary privilege; Roman citizenship was, in principle, an instrument of governance.

In the Andes, between the fifth and second centuries BCE, the Chavin horizon dissolves and the formative world fragments into regional traditions — Paracas on the south coast, with its funerary bundles and its iconography of decapitators; the developments that would lead into Nasca and Moche. The parallel with Greece is precise: in both cases the end of an integrating koine does not produce unification but a mosaic of competing regional powers, with growing militarization and a more explicit iconography of violence. And in both cases the later unification will come from a periphery that no one considered central: Macedonia in the Greek north, Wari and later Cusco in the Andean highlands. Centers rarely reinvent themselves; they tend to be replaced by their margins.

sections.heading: Resonances 2024–2026: rearmament, exhaustion, and elections without a project
paragraphs: Three contemporary resonances take this period out of the realm of archaeology. The first is rearmament. Greece has sustained for decades one of NATO's highest military expenditures as a proportion of its economy — above three percent of GDP — driven by the Turkish hypothesis, and signed in 2021 a mutual defense agreement with France alongside the purchase of frigates and fighter jets. Since 2022, and more intensely in 2024–2026, the entire European Union has been debating its own rearmament and the reconstruction of a strategic autonomy it does not have. The structure of the problem is the same as in 387 BCE: how the defense of a fragmented space is financed, who decides, and what is surrendered in exchange for protection. The guarantor has changed names — Susa, Washington, Brussels — but the question of the weak facing the strong, formulated at Melos, has not changed shape.

The second is the exhaustion of political forms. What we have described in this period — institutions that continue to function formally while losing the capacity to decide — is a diagnosis uncomfortably applicable to the present. In Greece, the two-party system that followed 1974 survived the 2010 crisis, but with eroded electoral participation and an institutional distrust that the mobilizations over the Tempi railway disaster laid bare in 2023 and 2025. In Peru, the general election of April 2026 was held amid an unprecedented fragmentation of candidacies and parliamentary blocs in republican history, after a decade in which Congress had turned presidential vacancy into an ordinary instrument of government. In both cases the formal machinery operates — there are elections, there are courts, there is alternation — and the capacity to produce lasting collective decisions has been hollowed out. It is the state of Greece in 350 BCE: a great deal of politics, very little sovereignty.

The third is more specific and more useful for the trip. Corcyra took part in the Second Athenian League from 375 BCE and tore itself apart again in an oligarchic-democratic civil war in 361 BCE: the island repeats its pattern, the geographic hinge becomes a factional hinge, because in a node of transit there is always a party of trade with the West and a party of alliance with the East. That pattern — local elites aligned with rival external powers, and a population that pays for the arbitration — is recognizable in any contemporary peripheral economy, including the Peruvian relationship among mining project, foreign capital, and community, where the dispute is never merely local even though the dead always are.
